chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Idris (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Sahban, from Abu Imran al-Armani, from Abdullah ibn al-Hakam, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him: There are people who, when something from the Quran is mentioned to them or they are told about it, one of them becomes so stunned that it seems as though if his hands and feet were cut off, he would not feel it.
He said: Glory be to God! That is from Satan. They were not commanded to do this. Rather, it is only softness, tenderness, tears, and awe.

key_terms.الدمعة: Tears -- the natural emotional response of a heart moved by divine words
key_terms.الرقة: Tenderness, delicacy of feeling -- emotional sensitivity without loss of self-control
key_terms.اللين: Softness, gentleness -- a quality of the heart when moved by scripture
key_terms.الوجل: Awe, reverential fear -- a deep, conscious trembling of the heart before God
key_terms.صعق: To become stunned, lose consciousness, faint -- used here for exaggerated ecstatic reactions

ai.seo_question: What is the correct emotional response to hearing the Quran according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Jabir asked Imam al-Baqir (AS) about people who fall unconscious or lose all sensation when hearing the Quran. The Imam condemned this extreme reaction as being from Satan, clarifying that the proper spiritual response to hearing the Quran should be inner softness, tender-heartedness, tearfulness, and reverent fear -- not theatrical fainting. This teaching was given in the early 2nd century AH when such dramatic displays of emotion during Quran recitation were practiced by some Sufi-influenced groups.
